title: The Gemini 3.5 "Snow Bunny" Leak
summary: The Gemini leak makes me think that leading-model performance may converge, and that long-term competitiveness will be decided by brand and developer ecosystems.
content:
The Gemini 3.5 "Snow Bunny" leak has X buzzing. At first glance, scenes pop up that make you think, "If this is real, isn't the game over?" But when I calmly take a step back, I come away with a slightly different thought.

To be honest, there's a good chance the lab versions at the companies building today's leading models are all this insane. In a competition where companies are burning through capital in the hundreds of trillions of won every year, it's hard to believe that one particular company suddenly achieved a transcendent result. If anything, there's also a strong possibility that the leak itself was intentional. A way of sending both the market and competitors the message, "This is how far we've come." Competition in today's leading-model market is also a fierce marketing battlefield, much like crypto, where you can't do anything if you can't get attention.

Everyone knows where Google has the advantage. Scale, data, infrastructure, TPUs, and cash flow. Its disadvantages come from exactly the same place. The responsibility demanded by that scale, and the standards of AI stability and completeness that responsibility forces on it. The paradox is that the company capable of running the fastest has to run the most carefully.

OpenAI has thoroughly enjoyed the benefits of being the first mover in branding. The equation "GPT = AI" still remains in the public mind, but the problem is that the validity period of that equation is shrinking very quickly.

Anthropic opened up a more advanced paradigm in coding. Still, even as someone who actively uses Claude Code in its current state, I find it difficult to answer readily when asked, "How long can this advantage really last?" Technical superiority and a business moat are different matters. The fact that it has failed to channel the developer energy of the present into an open ecosystem, as seen in incidents like the expulsion of Claude bots, is also a very significant risk.

xAI's Grok feels like Elon's will made tangible. It creates a presence by charging straight into areas competitors cautiously avoid, such as the bikini prompts covering X. Its positioning is closer to a culture war than a pure technology competition. The most frightening part is the religious gaslighting culture that willingly keeps developers from going home. I heard that the tents filling the office ahead of the Grok4 launch are still going strong. My younger sibling, who recently interviewed at Grok in Silicon Valley, ran away after seeing executives laughing as they pointed out a tent spot and said, "You can sleep there and work, too.".. (By contrast, they said OpenAI felt like a rich corporation.)

Gemini still lacks a clear brand narrative. It isn't the smartest AI, the freest AI, or the most developer-friendly AI. Being able to do everything well can also mean, put another way, that it still hasn't decided what it should do.

In the end, this race may be less a competition over model performance than a competition over what kind of worldview we can make people believe in. Technologies that seem incredible now will gradually converge and come closer to becoming public goods, and the real differences will ultimately emerge in the narratives. Things like Kimi, an open-source-based LLM, producing benchmarks on par with the major models in one shot will continue to happen. Who will be smiling a year from now? Which narrative will become the most durable, long-lasting moat and lock in its community?
